name: Bryn Celli Ddu
summary: A Neolithic passage tomb on Anglesey under a mound about 26 m across, with a passage aligned on the midsummer sunrise. Cadw describes an earlier bank-and-ditch enclosure with a stone circle on the same spot.
uncertainty: The dates are approximate (around 3000 BC is the usual estimate) and come from general knowledge, not from the Cadw page, which gives no years. Whether a henge really preceded the tomb is disputed; the end of use is not dated.

name: Barclodiad y Gawres
summary: A Neolithic passage tomb on the west coast of Anglesey. Several stones carry zig-zags and spirals like those in Irish tombs; Cadw notes Bryn Celli Ddu is the only other tomb in the UK with such art.
uncertainty: No radiocarbon date is cited here; about 3000 BC is the conventional estimate by analogy with the Irish tombs. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Pentre Ifan
summary: The best-preserved Neolithic portal dolmen in Wales: a capstone of about 16 tonnes on three uprights, once at the end of a cairn some 30 m long. Excavated by W. F. Grimes in 1936-7.
uncertainty: Not closely dated. Coflein says the Nevern valley dolmens were built about 6,000 years ago; Cadw says the capstone has stood for over 5,000 years. The start date here is a middle estimate and the end of use is a guess.

name: Tre'r Ceiri
summary: A stone-walled hillfort at about 480 m on Yr Eifl in Llŷn, crowded with some 150 round and sub-rectangular huts. Excavation shows it was probably built in the later Iron Age and stayed in use until at least the 4th century AD.
uncertainty: Coflein gives only 'later Iron Age' for the foundation and 'at least the 4th century' for the end; the years 200 BC and AD 400 are placeholders for those phrases. A Bronze Age cairn on the summit is older than the fort.

name: Great Orme copper mines
summary: Bronze Age copper mines in the limestone of the Great Orme, with kilometres of tunnels dug with bone and stone tools. Nineteen radiocarbon dates span about 1700-900 BC; a 2019 study argues for a boom about 1600-1400 BC that supplied metal across Britain and as far as the Baltic.
uncertainty: The boom model rests on metal chemistry and is one research group’s reading. Radiocarbon dates give ranges, not years. The marker is placed at the mine site from general knowledge of its position (Pleiades and Wikidata give only the headland).

name: Parys Mountain
summary: A copper-bearing hill in north Anglesey. Hammerstones and charcoal found in old workings point to Early Bronze Age mining; Roman working is inferred from stamped copper ingots found on Anglesey and Pleiades lists it as a Roman mine.
uncertainty: Weakly evidenced. The Bronze Age dates are radiocarbon ranges recalled from the literature, not fetched; Roman mining is an inference with no dated workings, and its start and end years are placeholders. Later opencast mining destroyed much of the evidence.

name: Llyn Cerrig Bach
summary: A small lake in west Anglesey where more than 150 iron and bronze objects, including chariot fittings, swords, spearheads and slave chains, were found in peat in 1942-3 during airfield building. They are read as offerings made over several centuries.
uncertainty: The objects were recovered from dredged peat, not excavated, so the span of deposition (about 300 BC to AD 100 on the style of the objects) is approximate, and any link with the Roman attack on Anglesey in AD 60 is conjecture. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Castell Henllys
summary: A small inland promontory fort in north Pembrokeshire, about 88 by 74 m, excavated over many seasons. The main gateway was begun in the 5th century BC; occupation inside ended about the turn of the era, when a settlement was set up in the annexe.
uncertainty: Coflein mentions a possible late or post-Roman reoccupation, which is not shown. The end date of the annexe settlement is a guess.

name: Caerleon
summary: One of three permanent legionary fortresses in Roman Britain, base of the Second Augustan Legion from about AD 75, with baths, barracks and an amphitheatre still visible. A Norman castle and small borough followed in the late 11th century.
uncertainty: Pleiades gives c. AD 75-300 for the legion’s base; how much of the legion remained after the late 3rd century, and what happened here between about 400 and the Norman castle (recorded in Domesday Book; 1086 is that date, recalled from general knowledge), is poorly known.

name: Segontium
summary: The main Roman fort of north-west Wales, founded under Agricola about AD 77 for a 1,000-strong auxiliary regiment and linked by road to Chester and Caerleon. Coins show it was held until about 394, longer than any other fort in Wales.
uncertainty: Cadw gives about AD 394 for the end, from coins; Pleiades gives c. 338. The later date is used here.

name: Carmarthen
summary: The westernmost town of Roman Britain, Moridunum, capital of the Demetae, with an amphitheatre. A royal castle was founded on the Tywi in the early 12th century and the borough became the centre of English royal government in south-west Wales.
uncertainty: Pleiades confirms only that Moridunum was the civitas capital of the Demetae. The fort date (c. AD 75), the change to a town (early 2nd century), the castle date (1109) and the claim that Carmarthen was the largest Welsh town in the later Middle Ages come from general knowledge. Continuity between about 400 and 1100 is not demonstrated.

name: Caerwent
summary: The Roman market town and administrative centre of the Silures, founded about AD 75-80. Its town walls, among the best preserved in northern Europe, still surround the village.
uncertainty: The town was small by the standards of Roman Britain (about 18 hectares). The pace of decline after the late 4th century is not well dated; an early medieval church community is recorded here but not shown as a separate phase.

name: Dolaucothi gold mines
summary: The only known Roman gold mine in Britain, at Pumsaint in Carmarthenshire: opencasts, adits and long aqueducts spread over at least a kilometre, beside a Roman fort.
uncertainty: Coflein says only that several features are thought to be Roman or earlier. Mining probably began soon after the conquest of the area in the 70s AD, but neither the start nor the end is dated and pre-Roman working is possible. The years are placeholders.

name: Nidum
summary: A Roman auxiliary fort on the west bank of the river Neath. Excavation shows a first fort of about AD 75-80, a smaller one of 80-90 held until about 125, reoccupation from about 140 to 170 and a late military phase about 275-320.
uncertainty: All dates are the excavators’ brackets as summarised by Coflein.

name: Abergavenny
summary: A Roman fort guarding the Usk valley road, known as Gobannium. A Norman lord built a castle and priory here in the late 11th century and a walled market town grew beside them.
uncertainty: Pleiades confirms only a fort and civil settlement. The fort’s dates (founded in the late 50s AD, given up in the 2nd century) and the castle date (c. 1087) are from general knowledge and are approximate.

name: Usk
summary: Site of an early legionary fortress, Burrium, built in the mid-50s AD during the war against the Silures and given up when the legion moved; Caerleon replaced it about AD 75. A Norman castle and planted borough followed in the 12th century.
uncertainty: Pleiades confirms only a Roman fort. The fortress dates (c. AD 55-67), the later small fort and the castle date are from general knowledge; the later two are rough.

name: Canovium
summary: A Roman auxiliary fort at Caerhun, guarding the crossing of the Conwy on the road from Chester to Caernarfon. It was occupied, with breaks, from Agricola’s campaign of AD 77/8 into the 4th century.
uncertainty: The breaks in occupation are not shown, and the end date is a placeholder for ‘the 4th century’.

name: Tomen y Mur
summary: An upland Roman fort in Meirionnydd with a rare set of surrounding earthworks: a small amphitheatre, parade ground, bath-house and practice camps. A castle mound was later raised inside it.
uncertainty: Coflein dates the fort to the late 1st century, ‘occupied into the 2nd century if not later’, and the mound to the 12th or 13th century, possibly after Norman armies camped here in the late 11th or early 12th. The years used are placeholders within those ranges.

name: Y Gaer, Brecon
summary: A Roman fort west of Brecon, founded about AD 75 where two main roads met and garrisoned by a Spanish cavalry regiment, the Vettones.
uncertainty: The foundation date is Cadw’s. The end date is a guess; later Roman use was intermittent. The position is from general knowledge of the site.

name: St Davids
summary: The monastery founded by St David in the 6th century became the leading church of Wales and, under Norman bishops from 1115, a cathedral. The present church was begun in 1181; a 12th-century pope ruled two pilgrimages here equal to one to Rome, and Bishop Henry de Gower built the great palace in 1328-47.
uncertainty: Nothing of the early monastery has been found and its foundation date is traditional. Only the papal privilege and the palace dates come from the Cadw page; 1115 (first Norman bishop) and 1181 (present cathedral begun) are from general knowledge. The shrine was dismantled at the Reformation, which is not shown as a phase.

name: Llantwit Major
summary: Llanilltud Fawr, the monastery of St Illtud in the Vale of Glamorgan, was remembered as the great school of early Christian Wales; the 7th-century Life of St Samson is the earliest witness. Carved stones of the 9th-11th centuries commemorate kings of Glywysing.
uncertainty: The foundation date follows the Dictionary of Welsh Biography’s floruit for Illtud (c. 475-525) and is approximate. No early monastic buildings have been found. The Norman takeover date is rounded.

name: Bangor
summary: A monastery founded by St Deiniol in the 6th century, the seat of the bishops of Gwynedd. The cathedral was rebuilt in stone in the 12th century and damaged in the wars of 1211, 1282 and 1402.
uncertainty: The Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives Deiniol’s death as 584 and notes it may really be 572; the foundation year is a guess within his lifetime. The 12th-century rebuilding and the war damage are from general knowledge.

name: Llandaff
summary: A church on the Taff associated with Saints Teilo, Dyfrig and Euddogwy. Bishop Urban began the present cathedral in 1120 and the Book of Llandaff was compiled to back its claims.
uncertainty: The early history rests on 12th-century documents written to support the bishopric; the start date is a placeholder. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Deganwy
summary: Twin hills above the Conwy estuary: by tradition the seat of Maelgwn, king of Gwynedd, in the 6th century. It was burnt by lightning in 812 and destroyed by the English in 822. Robert of Rhuddlan held it in the late 11th century; Henry III built a great castle in 1245-50, which Llywelyn ap Gruffudd destroyed in 1263.
uncertainty: The link with Maelgwn is tradition supported by 5th-6th-century imported pottery; the start date is a placeholder. Coflein notes the borough was still active in 1305, which is not shown.

name: Dinefwr
summary: A castle above the Tywi near Llandeilo, thought to have been founded in the later 12th century by the Lord Rhys and remembered as the principal court of Deheubarth. The standing remains are 13th and early 14th century.
uncertainty: The Welsh law-books name Dinefwr as the chief court of the south, but no remains older than the 12th century are known, so no earlier phase is shown. The dates 1165 and 1277 (taken by Edward I) are from general knowledge; Coflein says it was still maintained in the early 15th century and may have been replaced by Newton House later that century.

name: Mathrafal
summary: An earthwork enclosure and mound on the river Banwy, named in later tradition as the chief court of the kings of Powys.
uncertainty: Excavation in 1989 did not find an early medieval royal site: the mound belongs with an oval enclosure filled in by about 1310-1430, the square enclosure was built after about 1200, and the ‘royal court’ tradition is traced only to the mid 13th century. It is shown here only for its 13th-century phase.

name: Aberffraw
summary: By tradition the chief seat of the kings of Gwynedd, on the west coast of Anglesey; the princes styled themselves ‘prince of Aberffraw’ in the 13th century. The settlement declined after a great storm in 1331 altered the coast.
uncertainty: Coflein reports the royal seat as tradition. The position of the llys within the village is not securely established and the start date is a placeholder; documentary references begin in the 7th-9th centuries.

name: Dinas Emrys
summary: A rocky stronghold above Nant Gwynant, the legendary site of Vortigern’s fortress and Merlin’s dragons. Excavations in 1910 and 1954-6 found Iron Age, Roman and early medieval occupation; a stone tower was added at the end of the 12th century.
uncertainty: The phases of occupation are not closely dated and the years are placeholders. The Vortigern story is 9th-century legend.

name: Llangorse crannog
summary: The only crannog (artificial island) known in Wales, built in Llangorse Lake for the king of Brycheiniog from timbers felled between AD 889 and 893. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that a Mercian army sent by Æthelflæd destroyed ‘Brecenanmere’ in 916 and took the king’s wife captive.
uncertainty: The identification of ‘Brecenanmere’ with the crannog is probable, not certain.

name: Dinas Powys hillfort
summary: A small defended hilltop near Cardiff, excavated by Leslie Alcock in the 1950s. Imported Mediterranean and Gaulish pottery, glass and fine metalworking show a wealthy household of the 5th to 7th centuries.
uncertainty: The dating of the ramparts has been revised more than once and the end date is approximate. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Pillar of Eliseg
summary: The shaft of a 9th-century cross near Llangollen, set up by Cyngen, king of Powys (died 854/5), in honour of his great-grandfather Eliseg. Its long Latin inscription, now illegible, traced the dynasty’s descent.
uncertainty: Cadw’s page dates the pillar only to the 9th century; the attribution to Cyngen depends on a transcript of the inscription made in 1696, and the year shown is a placeholder within his reign.

name: Chepstow
summary: A castle on a cliff above the Wye, begun in 1067 by William fitz Osbern, earl of Hereford, and one of the first Norman strongholds in Wales. Its great tower is among the oldest stone castle buildings in Britain; a walled port town grew beside it.
uncertainty: Some scholars date the great tower to William I’s visit of 1081 or later, not to fitz Osbern.

name: Pembroke
summary: A castle on a tidal promontory, established by the Normans about 1093-4 and never taken by the Welsh. The round great tower was built at the start of the 13th century; Henry Tudor, later Henry VII, was born here in 1457.
uncertainty: Coflein gives ‘about 1094’ for the foundation. The link of the great tower with William Marshal and the birth of Henry VII are from general knowledge.

name: Cardiff
summary: A series of Roman forts stood beside the Taff from the late 50s AD to the late 4th century. About 1081 William I set a castle inside the walls of the last fort, and the borough beside it became the head of the lordship of Glamorgan and one of the larger towns in Wales.
uncertainty: The date of the stone fort (late 3rd century) and the size of the medieval town are from general knowledge; the Roman name is uncertain (Pleiades offers ‘Tamion?’). Nothing is known of the site between the 4th and 11th centuries.

name: Caerphilly Castle
summary: The largest castle in Wales, begun in 1268 by Gilbert de Clare, lord of Glamorgan, against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. Its concentric walls and wide artificial lakes were new to Britain.
uncertainty: The date by which the castle was ruinous is approximate (it was derelict when John Leland saw it in the 1530s).

name: Dolwyddelan Castle
summary: A stone keep guarding a route through Snowdonia, built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, ruler of Gwynedd from 1201 to 1240. It fell to Edward I in 1283, who refitted it.
uncertainty: The building date is not recorded; 1210 is a placeholder within Llywelyn’s reign. The castle was lived in again from the late 15th century, which is not shown.

name: Castell y Bere
summary: A castle on a rock in the Dysynni valley, begun in 1221 by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth to guard the southern border of Gwynedd. It was taken by Edward I’s forces in 1283 and given up after the Welsh rising of 1294.

name: Dolbadarn Castle
summary: A round stone tower at the foot of the Llanberis pass, most likely built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth in the late 12th or early 13th century.
uncertainty: Cadw gives only ‘late 12th or early 13th century’; 1210 is a placeholder. The end date reflects the removal of its timber to Caernarfon in 1284, a detail from general knowledge.

name: Criccieth Castle
summary: A castle on a headland in Cardigan Bay. Llywelyn ap Iorwerth built the twin-towered gatehouse, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd added the outer ward, Edward I refitted it, and Owain Glyndŵr burnt it in 1404.
uncertainty: The first building date is not recorded; about 1230 is the usual estimate, from general knowledge.

name: Flint
summary: The first of Edward I’s castles in Wales, begun in 1277 and largely finished by 1284, with a planned borough beside it. Richard II met Henry Bolingbroke here in 1399.

name: Rhuddlan
summary: The lowest crossing of the Clwyd. Edward the Elder founded a burh here in 921; it was Gruffudd ap Llywelyn’s seat until 1063; Robert of Rhuddlan raised a motte in 1073. Edward I began the present concentric castle in 1277 and issued the Statute of Rhuddlan here in 1284.
uncertainty: Only the 1277 date comes from Cadw and the Statute from the Bodleian guide. The burh of ‘Cledemutha’ (921), Gruffudd’s court and the motte of 1073 are from general knowledge; the identification of Cledemutha with Rhuddlan is generally, not universally, accepted.

name: Conwy
summary: Edward I and Master James of St George built the castle and a 1.3 km circuit of town walls here between 1283 and 1287. The site had been the Cistercian abbey of Aberconwy, burial place of Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, which the king moved up the valley to Maenan.
uncertainty: The abbey phase (founded 1186, on this site from the 1190s) is from general knowledge.

name: Caernarfon
summary: Edward I began the castle and walled borough in 1283, with a quay, all at once; work lasted 47 years and was still unfinished about 1330. It was the centre of royal government in North Wales. The castle was in decay by the 16th century.
uncertainty: The Norman motte of about 1090 and the Welsh court that followed are from general knowledge and their dates are approximate.

name: Harlech Castle
summary: A concentric castle on a crag above Cardigan Bay, begun in May 1283 and largely complete by 1289. Owain Glyndŵr took it in 1404 and kept his court and family here until it was retaken in 1409; it fell again to the Yorkists in 1468 after a long siege.

name: Beaumaris
summary: The last of Edward I’s Welsh castles, begun in 1295 after the rising of Madog ap Llywelyn. Money ran short and work petered out by the 1320s, leaving the towers below their planned height. The borough became the main port of Anglesey.
uncertainty: Glyndŵr’s supporters held it from 1403 for about two years, which is not shown as a phase.

name: Kidwelly
summary: A Norman ringwork of the early 12th century, rebuilt in stone as a concentric castle in the late 13th and 14th centuries. The Lord Rhys captured it in 1159.
uncertainty: Cadw gives only ‘early 12th century’; 1106 (the grant to Bishop Roger of Salisbury) is from general knowledge.

name: Montgomery
summary: Henry III began the stone castle about 1223 against Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, replacing the nearby timber castle of Hen Domen. It withstood attacks in 1228, 1231 and 1245. The treaty that recognised Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales was sealed at the nearby ford in 1267.
uncertainty: The marker is at the stone castle; Hen Domen lies about 1.5 km north-west. Its foundation about 1071 by Roger of Montgomery is from general knowledge.

name: Dolforwyn Castle
summary: A castle built by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1273 on a ridge above the Severn, in defiance of the king and facing royal Montgomery. Roger Mortimer took it in 1277 after a two-week siege.
uncertainty: Cadw says only that it was abandoned in the 14th century; the end year is a placeholder.

name: Raglan Castle
summary: A late medieval fortress-palace in Gwent. Sir William ap Thomas built the moated Great Tower about 1435 and his son William Herbert, earl of Pembroke, enlarged it.
uncertainty: An earlier manor stood here; it is not shown.

name: Denbigh
summary: A Welsh princely residence of Dafydd ap Gruffudd, whose attack on Hawarden in 1282 set off Edward I’s final war. Henry de Lacy then built a large castle and walled town on the site; the half-built castle was captured in the rising of 1294.
uncertainty: The start date of the Welsh court is a placeholder. The position is from general knowledge.

name: Sycharth
summary: A motte and bailey in the Cynllaith valley, the chief home of Owain Glyndŵr. A poem of about 1390 praises its fine timber hall on a green mound; it was burnt in 1403 and has no later history.
uncertainty: Coflein says the castle may be as early as the 12th century but direct evidence is lacking; the start date here marks only the 14th-century hall.

name: Castell Dinas Brân
summary: A hilltop castle above Llangollen, built inside an Iron Age hillfort by the rulers of northern Powys in the 1260s and burnt by its own garrison before Edward I’s army in 1277.
uncertainty: The building date is an estimate. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Tintern Abbey
summary: The first Cistercian abbey in Wales, founded in 1131 on the Wye. The great church was begun in 1269. The abbey surrendered in 1536 in the first round of the dissolution.

name: Strata Florida Abbey
summary: A Cistercian abbey in the Ceredigion uplands, founded in 1164 by a Norman lord and soon taken under the patronage of the Lord Rhys. The monks entered their new church in 1201. Welsh princes were buried here and it supported the Welsh cause; it closed by 1539.
uncertainty: The first community may have begun on a different site nearby before moving here in the 1180s; the marker is at the later abbey.

name: Valle Crucis Abbey
summary: A Cistercian abbey near Llangollen, founded in 1201 by Madog ap Gruffudd, prince of northern Powys, and named after the nearby Pillar of Eliseg. It was dissolved in 1537.

name: Neath Abbey
summary: Founded in 1130 by the Norman knight Richard de Granville; by the late 13th century one of the wealthiest abbeys in Wales.
uncertainty: The dissolution year (1539) and the abbey’s first affiliation to Savigny are from general knowledge; Cadw’s page gives neither.

name: Margam Abbey
summary: A Cistercian abbey founded about 1147 and dissolved in 1536, thought to stand on an earlier monastic site: early Christian carved stones were found around it. The western part of the nave survives as the parish church.

name: Basingwerk Abbey
summary: An abbey near Holywell on the Dee estuary, founded in 1131 and much rebuilt in the 13th century. Wat’s Dyke reaches the estuary close by.
uncertainty: The dissolution year is from general knowledge. The first community may have been at a different site nearby.

name: Swansea
summary: The castle at the mouth of the Tawe was founded in or soon after 1106 as the head of the Norman lordship of Gower; a borough and port grew beside it. The first castle was earth and timber, rebuilt in stone probably between 1221 and 1284.
uncertainty: Size is a rough judgement; medieval Swansea had perhaps 1,000-2,000 people. A Norse origin for the name is often suggested but no Viking-age settlement has been found.

name: Haverfordwest
summary: A castle founded about 1110 by Tancred, a Fleming, at the tidal limit of the Western Cleddau. The town below it became one of the largest and richest in medieval Wales.
uncertainty: The town’s later size is from general knowledge; it was made a county in itself in the late 15th or 16th century.

name: Brecon
summary: Bernard de Neufmarché defeated the king of Brycheiniog near here in 1093 and built a castle and a Benedictine priory (now the cathedral) at the meeting of the Usk and Honddu. A walled town followed.
uncertainty: The marker is at the priory church. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Wrexham
summary: A market town on the Welsh side of the border, first recorded in the 12th century. It was never a chartered walled borough but by the 16th century was among the most populous towns in Wales.
uncertainty: The first mention (a castle at ‘Wristlesham’, 1161) and the growth of the town are from general knowledge; the phase dates are approximate.

name: Aberystwyth
summary: Edward I’s brother Edmund began the castle and borough in 1277, at first called Llanbadarn. Owain Glyndŵr held it from 1404 to 1408.
uncertainty: An earlier castle of the same name stood about 2 km to the south. The Dictionary of Welsh Biography confirms Glyndŵr’s capture of Aberystwyth in 1404; the other dates are from general knowledge.

name: Monmouth
summary: William fitz Osbern built a castle where the Monnow meets the Wye soon after 1066; a priory and walled town followed. Henry V was born in the castle in 1386 or 1387. A Roman fort, Blestium, had stood here.
uncertainty: The Roman fort is not shown as a phase. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Machynlleth
summary: A small market town in the Dyfi valley, with a market charter of 1291. By tradition Owain Glyndŵr was crowned Prince of Wales and held a parliament here in 1404.
uncertainty: The 1404 parliament rests on later tradition and a few contemporary references; the ‘Parliament House’ shown in the town is a later building. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

name: Battle of Mynydd Carn
summary: In 1081 Gruffudd ap Cynan, returning from exile in Ireland, and Rhys ap Tewdwr defeated and killed Trahaearn ap Caradog, Caradog ap Gruffudd and Meilyr ap Rhiwallon. The victory secured Gwynedd for Gruffudd’s line and Deheubarth for Rhys’s.
uncertainty: The battlefield has not been found. Sources place it a day’s march from St Davids at a hill with a cairn; the marker uses the grid reference in the Coflein record, which is one suggestion among several in Pembrokeshire.

name: Battle of Crug Mawr
summary: In 1136 Owain and Cadwaladr of Gwynedd with Gruffudd ap Rhys routed a Norman and Flemish army near Cardigan; many of the defeated drowned in the Teifi. It was the largest Welsh victory of the rising that followed Henry I’s death.
uncertainty: Gerald of Wales places the battle at the hill of Crug Mawr (probably Banc-y-Warren, used for the marker); a Welsh chronicle suggests it was fought nearer Cardigan castle and the river.

name: Battle of Orewin Bridge
summary: On 11 December 1282 the king’s forces with Roger Mortimer and Gruffudd ap Gwenwynwyn came on the Welsh army without warning near Builth. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, and his leading men were killed; native rule in Wales ended within months.
uncertainty: Only Walter of Guisborough gives a location (a bridge and ford on the Irfon), and his account resembles his own description of Stirling Bridge. The marker uses Coflein’s grid reference; where and how Llywelyn died is disputed.

name: Battle of Bryn Glas
summary: On 22 June 1402 Owain Glyndŵr’s men defeated the levies of Herefordshire at Pilleth in Maelienydd and captured Edmund Mortimer, who then joined Glyndŵr’s cause.
uncertainty: Chronicles name the hill of Bryn Glas west of Pilleth church, but fieldwork there has found no trace of the fighting and other sources point to neighbouring hills.

name: Battle of Bryn Derwin
summary: In 1255 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd defeated his brothers Owain and Dafydd and became sole ruler of Gwynedd west of the Conwy, the first step toward his principality.
uncertainty: The battlefield is not located; the marker is at the pass of Bwlch Derwin on the border of Arfon and Eifionydd, the usual identification, placed from general knowledge.

name: Stonehenge
summary: The ditch and bank were dug about 3000 BCE and the great stones set up about 2500 BCE. The bluestones were rearranged two or three centuries later and the last known digging, the Y and Z holes, dates to 1800-1500 BCE.
uncertainty: Phase boundaries are rounded radiocarbon estimates. How long it stayed in active use after 1500 BCE is not known.

name: Durrington Walls
summary: A very large late Neolithic settlement beside the Avon, later enclosed by Britain's largest henge. It is linked to the building of the sarsen phase at Stonehenge, 3 km away.
uncertainty: Dates are rounded from memory of the Stonehenge Riverside Project results (settlement about 2500 BCE, in use for only a few decades). Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Avebury
summary: The largest stone circle in Britain, inside a huge henge ditch, built and altered from about 2850 to about 2200 BCE. Its monuments were abandoned around 1800 BCE.
uncertainty: Internal sequence of the circles and avenues is not closely dated.

name: Silbury Hill
summary: The largest artificial prehistoric mound in Europe, probably raised over a short period between about 2470 and 2350 BCE. Its purpose is unknown.
uncertainty: No burial has been found; the function is a matter of conjecture.

name: West Kennet Long Barrow
summary: One of the largest Neolithic chambered tombs in Britain, built around 3650 BCE, used for at least a thousand years and blocked with great sarsens around 2000 BCE.
uncertainty: Construction date is a modelled radiocarbon estimate; the date of final blocking is approximate. Dates are English Heritage's round figures.

name: Windmill Hill
summary: The largest known Neolithic causewayed enclosure, three rings of interrupted ditch on a low hill near Avebury.
uncertainty: Start date is a modelled estimate; the length of use is uncertain. Dates are English Heritage's figures: built around 3675 BCE, in use until around 2500 BCE, largely abandoned by the end of the third millennium.

name: Hambledon Hill
summary: A chalk spur in Dorset used twice: as a large early Neolithic enclosure complex and, three thousand years later, as a multivallate hillfort.
uncertainty: Both date ranges are approximate; the end of Iron Age occupation is not well fixed. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Cissbury
summary: Among the earliest flint mines in Britain, with over 200 shafts on the South Downs, later enclosed by one of the largest hillforts in Sussex.
uncertainty: The mines began around or soon after 4000 BCE; all four dates are rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Langdale axe quarries
summary: High fell-side quarries whose green volcanic stone was made into polished axes found all over Britain.
uncertainty: Date range is approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Castlerigg
summary: A ring of 38 stones among the Lake District fells, probably raised in the late Neolithic.
uncertainty: Never securely dated by excavation. English Heritage puts it at about 4,500 years ago; Aubrey Burl's case for about 3200 BCE, which would make it one of the earliest circles in Britain, is described there as not strongly supported.

name: Thornborough Henges
summary: Three large henges in a line across the Ure-Swale plain, the largest ritual complex between the Thames and Orkney.
uncertainty: Not closely dated. English Heritage says the three henges were built about 4,500 to 5,000 years ago, over an older cursus, and stayed a focus for burials into the early Bronze Age (a nearby timber row is put at 1800-1600 BCE). The end date here is a judgement.

name: Arbor Low
summary: A henge and recumbent stone circle on the White Peak limestone plateau.
uncertainty: Not closely dated. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Grime's Graves
summary: A field of more than 400 late Neolithic flint mine shafts in the Norfolk Breckland, worked from about 2600 to about 2100 BCE.

name: Holme timber circle (Seahenge)
summary: A ring of 55 split oak posts around an inverted tree stump, built on a saltmarsh. Tree rings show the timbers were felled in 2049 BCE.
uncertainty: The felling date is precise; how long the circle was used is unknown, so the end date is nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Flag Fen
summary: A kilometre-long post alignment and timber platform across the fen edge near Peterborough, built in stages between about 1365 and 967 BCE and used for ritual deposits long afterwards.
uncertainty: End of use is approximate (deposits continued for more than 1,200 years in all). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Must Farm
summary: A small late Bronze Age settlement of round houses on stilts over a fen channel, destroyed by fire very soon after it was built and preserved in the silt.
uncertainty: Built about 850 BCE; the year is approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Grimspound
summary: The best-known of the Bronze Age enclosed settlements on Dartmoor, part of a moor then divided by long field boundaries (reaves).
uncertainty: Never dated by modern excavation; the range is the conventional one. English Heritage gives 'probably late Bronze Age (about 1500-800 BC)' and notes the settlement pattern was changing by about 1000 BCE; there is still no radiocarbon date.

name: Uffington White Horse and Castle
summary: A 110 m stylised horse cut into the chalk of the Berkshire Downs, with an early Iron Age hillfort on the ridge above.
uncertainty: English Heritage reports the horse as dated to the later Bronze Age or Iron Age, between 1740 and 210 BCE; the start date used here sits inside that bracket and is not a measurement. The hillfort's 700 BCE start is from memory.

name: Maiden Castle
summary: The largest hillfort in Britain. In the middle Iron Age (about 400-120 BCE) it was the main settlement of southern Dorset; by the Roman invasion it was almost empty.
uncertainty: The story of a Roman assault in 44 CE is now questioned. The end of the temple is not dated; 430 is nominal.

name: Danebury
summary: The most thoroughly excavated hillfort in Britain, with streets of round houses and thousands of grain storage pits; perhaps 200-350 people lived inside.
uncertainty: Population is an excavator's estimate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Cadbury Castle
summary: A Somerset hillfort reoccupied on a large scale in the late 5th and 6th centuries, one of the strongest pieces of evidence for post-Roman British lordship in the south-west.
uncertainty: All dates are rounded from excavation reports recalled from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Glastonbury Lake Village
summary: A waterlogged Iron Age village in the Somerset Levels, exceptionally well preserved.
uncertainty: Date range approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Hengistbury Head
summary: The main known port of late Iron Age Britain before Caesar: Italian wine, glass and figs came in, and metals went out to Armorica.
uncertainty: The peak is inferred from wine amphorae, most of which predate 50 BCE. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Stanwick
summary: Some 300 hectares of earthworks in North Yorkshire, probably the seat of the Brigantian rulers who were clients of Rome until about 69 CE.
uncertainty: The link to Queen Cartimandua is an inference; dates are approximate. English Heritage dates the ramparts to the 1st century CE, with occupation from the middle of the century and decline after 70; the start year 40 is approximate.

name: London
summary: Founded about 47-50 CE, burned in 60/61, the largest town of Roman Britain, then almost deserted for two centuries. From the late 9th century it grew back inside its Roman walls and by 1377 had about three times as many taxpayers as any other English town.
uncertainty: Sizes are relative ranks, not populations. Descend into the London site for dated, sourced detail. Roman dates checked against the London Museum timeline (founded 47-50, burned 60-61, wall 200-220, end 400-410) and English Heritage (founded about 50, wall about 200). Post-Roman dates and all sizes still rest on Wikipedia and judgement.

name: Colchester
summary: The chief centre of late Iron Age Britain, then a legionary fortress and the first Roman colonia, burned by Boudica in 60/61. It was tenth among English towns in the 1377 poll tax.
uncertainty: Coin use ends in the early 5th century; what followed is obscure. Fortress (c. 44), colony (c. 49-50), the Boudican fire (60-1), walls built after the fire, 917 and the castle of the 1070s are from VCH Essex vol. 9. The 20 BCE start, the 275 step and the phase sizes are judgement.

name: St Albans
summary: The third great town of Roman Britain by tradition, burned by Boudica in 61. The medieval abbey and town grew on the hill outside the Roman walls, around the supposed grave of Britain's first martyr.
uncertainty: Roman occupation ended between about 400 and 450. The abbey's foundation by Offa about 793 is a later tradition. English Heritage confirms the Boudican destruction about 60 and a town wall built 265-270. Other dates, including Offa's foundation of the abbey (a later tradition), are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: York
summary: Founded as a legionary fortress in 71. Two emperors died here and Constantine was proclaimed here in 306. It was the Viking capital of the north from 866/7 to 954 and the second town of England in 1377.
uncertainty: The 5th and 6th centuries are almost blank. York had slipped to about fifteenth by wealth in the 1520s. 71, 627, 735, 866 and 954 are confirmed by VCH City of York, which attributes the colonia to Severus. Later rankings follow tax tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Lincoln
summary: A fortress of about 60 CE turned into a colonia for veterans, probably in 86. It revived under Danish rule and stood among the four or five largest English towns from Domesday to the 13th century.
uncertainty: The colonia date is the favoured estimate, not a recorded one. Whether Lincoln was a 4th-century provincial capital is debated. The move of the see to Lincoln in 1072 is confirmed by English Heritage. Roman and Danish dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Gloucester
summary: A colonia founded under Nerva at the lowest crossing of the Severn. It was eighth by Russell's Domesday estimate and seventeenth in 1377.
uncertainty: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's capture of Gloucester in 577 is a late and doubtful record. The 679 and c. 900 dates are from memory. The minster of about 679-81, Aethelflaed's refoundation (fortified by 902-14, St Oswald's by 909) and the see of 1541 are from VCH Gloucester. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Chester
summary: Begun in the mid 70s as the largest legionary fortress in Britain and held until the late 4th or early 5th century. Refortified in 907, it became the seat of a Norman marcher earldom.
uncertainty: The date of the legion's departure is not known. 74, about 90 and 907 are from VCH Cheshire; 1071 for the earldom is from memory.

name: Wroxeter
summary: Founded as a military base about 47 and refounded as a city in the 90s. At 78 hectares it was one of the largest cities of Roman Britain. It was never built over.
uncertainty: The centre was abandoned by the mid 5th century; claims of grand timber rebuilding into the 6th or 7th century are now doubted.

name: Silchester
summary: An Iron Age centre founded about 20-10 BCE which became a Roman town and, unusually, was never reoccupied.
uncertainty: English Heritage puts the abandonment 'sometime between AD 550 and 650'; 600 is the midpoint.

name: Richborough
summary: Widely believed to be the landing place of 43 CE and long the formal gateway to Britain. The town was cleared after 250 for a fort, rebuilt in stone in 275-290.
uncertainty: The arch is dated only to between 85 and 150. Coins show activity into the early 5th century.

name: Canterbury
summary: Roman capital of Kent, then from 597 the centre of the English church. It was fourteenth in the 1377 poll tax and tenth by wealth in the 1520s.
uncertainty: How much life continued inside the walls between about 420 and 597 is disputed. St Augustine's Abbey was dissolved in 1538 (from memory). 597-8 (English Heritage, St Augustine's), Becket's murder in 1170 and the end of the priory in 1540 (VCH Kent) are confirmed. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Winchester
summary: Roman Venta, refounded by Alfred with a new street grid and the largest burh in the Burghal Hidage. It was second only to London at Domesday but thirtieth in the 1377 poll tax.
uncertainty: Domesday omits Winchester, so its 11th-century size is an estimate (about 6,000). The 880 date for the replanning is approximate. VCH Hampshire gives the Old Minster's foundation as 643 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) or 639 (Winchester Annals); 648 here follows another Chronicle reading. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Cirencester
summary: Civitas capital of the Dobunni and, on the usual reconstruction, capital of the 4th-century province of Britannia Prima.
uncertainty: Its role as a provincial capital is an inference from one inscription. English Heritage dates the amphitheatre to the early 2nd century and notes the Chronicle's capture of 577. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Bath
summary: A sanctuary and bathing complex around the hot spring, not an ordinary town. The Roman Baths' own timeline has the buildings collapsing by about 500 and a Saxon church founded in 675.
uncertainty: The temple is usually dated to the 60s-70s; the museum timeline only says the Romans came to Bath about 50. VCH Somerset dates the nunnery charter to 676, a year later than the museum timeline, and puts the bishop's move to Bath in 1088.

name: Exeter
summary: The western end of the Fosse Way, held successively as fortress, Roman town, burh and cathedral city. It ranked 24th in 1377 and 6th in the 1520s.
uncertainty: Fortress and town dates are rounded from memory. Rankings are from tax records, which measure taxpayers or wealth. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Leicester
summary: Civitas capital of the Corieltauvi and later one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. It ranked eighteenth in 1377.
uncertainty: Roman dates are approximate. English Heritage: occupied soon after 43, street grid and civitas capital by the 2nd century, baths about 160, peak in the late 3rd century; the year 50 is approximate. Danish and later dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Chichester
summary: Roman capital of the client kingdom of Togidubnus and its successor civitas, refortified as a burh and made a bishop's seat in 1075.
uncertainty: VCH Sussex has Chichester a burh of some importance by 894-5 and confirms the move of the see from Selsey. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Fishbourne Roman Palace
summary: The largest Roman residence known north of the Alps, commonly linked to the client king Togidubnus.
uncertainty: The owner is not attested. Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Dorchester
summary: Founded about 70 CE, after nearby Maiden Castle had emptied.
uncertainty: Post-Roman history is poorly known; the 900 date is nominal.

name: Caistor St Edmund
summary: A small Roman town laid out in Iceni territory after the Boudican revolt and never built over.
uncertainty: End date uncertain; some activity continued into the Anglo-Saxon period. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Aldborough
summary: The northernmost civitas capital of Roman Britain: a trading settlement from about 70, laid out as a planned town about 120 and walled in stone in the late 2nd century.
uncertainty: Foundation date approximate. Foundation and planning dates are English Heritage's; the end of town life is not dated.

name: Carlisle
summary: The Roman town at the west end of the frontier. It was taken into the English kingdom only in 1092.
uncertainty: The first fort is tree-ring dated to 72/3 (from memory). The centuries between 876 and 1092 are obscure. English Heritage gives the first fort as AD 72 and William II's castle as 1092. The 876 desertion and the 1133 bishopric are from memory.

name: Brough-on-Humber
summary: Usually taken to be the civitas centre of the Parisi, on the strength of one theatre inscription.
uncertainty: Status and dates are uncertain. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Water Newton
summary: A walled small town at the centre of the Nene Valley pottery industry; the earliest Christian silver plate from the Roman empire was found here.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Catterick
summary: A Roman fort and town at the Swale crossing; Bede names it as a place where Paulinus baptised.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Corbridge
summary: The most northerly town of the Roman empire, where Dere Street crossed the Tyne.
uncertainty: Dates rounded. Fort and town dates are English Heritage's (first fort on this site about 86, legionary base and town from the 160s).

name: Vindolanda
summary: A fort built before Hadrian's Wall and rebuilt nine times. Its ink writing tablets, of about 100 CE, are the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.
uncertainty: The Vindolanda Trust says only that the first fort predates the Wall and that the site was finally abandoned in the 9th century; 85 is the usual estimate.

name: Housesteads
summary: Built within a decade of 122 for an 800-strong infantry regiment, and held to the end of the 4th century.
uncertainty: The garrison may have stayed into the early 5th century; the end date is nominal.

name: Chesters
summary: Built about 124 for a 500-strong cavalry regiment and occupied until the Roman army left Britain.

name: Birdoswald
summary: A Wall fort where large timber halls show a community staying on under local leaders after Roman pay stopped.
uncertainty: The post-Roman halls are dated only loosely. English Heritage: the site was cleared for the Wall in 122 and the fort finished before 138. The post-Roman hall dates are from memory.

name: South Shields
summary: The sea port of Hadrian's Wall, turned into a granary depot for the Severan campaigns in Scotland.
uncertainty: Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Dover
summary: The shortest crossing to Gaul. The Roman lighthouse of about 130 still stands inside the castle, whose great tower Henry II built in 1179-89; the castle held out against a French siege in 1216-17.
uncertainty: The fleet-base and shore-fort dates are from memory; Domesday suggests about 2,000 people.

name: Portchester
summary: The best preserved Roman fort north of the Alps, reused as a burh and a medieval castle.
uncertainty: The Latin name is an identification, not a certainty. English Heritage: built probably between 285 and 290 (coins date it after about 268), occupied through the 5th century, given to the king in 904, castle built in one corner after the Conquest. The year 1100 for the castle is approximate.

name: Pevensey
summary: Built about 290 (tree-ring date). William of Normandy landed here on 28 September 1066 and a medieval castle grew within the Roman circuit.
uncertainty: English Heritage gives 471 for the Saxon storming recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; the Chronicle's own year is 491 and neither is reliable.

name: Burgh Castle
summary: A shore fort overlooking the wide estuary that then covered the lower Yare and Waveney.
uncertainty: Date approximate. English Heritage: built in the late 3rd century; Bede's monastery of St Fursa (about 630) may have been here.

name: Reculver
summary: An early Saxon Shore fort guarding the channel that then made Thanet an island; a Kentish minster was founded in it in 669.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Dates are English Heritage's: fort of the early 3rd century, monastery founded 669, no longer monastic by the 10th century.

name: Rochester
summary: Where Watling Street crossed the Medway. England's second-oldest see was founded here in 604.
uncertainty: 604 and 1080 are from VCH Kent. Roman dates are from memory, as is the keep (about 1127).

name: Manchester
summary: A Roman fort, then for centuries a minor place. It is included to show how small the later industrial cities still were in 1625.
uncertainty: All dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Lancaster
summary: A Roman fort site that became the castle and shire town of a county palatine.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Charterhouse-on-Mendip
summary: Lead was being mined on Mendip under army control within six years of the invasion: stamped ingots are dated to 49 CE.
uncertainty: End of Roman working and the restart of medieval mining are approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Wirksworth
summary: Centre of the Peak District lead field, worked in the Roman period and recorded again from the 8th century and in Domesday.
uncertainty: That Wirksworth is Roman Lutudarum is probable but unproven; all dates are nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Tintagel
summary: A defended headland with more imported 5th-7th century Mediterranean pottery than any other site in Britain, probably a seat of the rulers of Dumnonia.
uncertainty: Its exact status is inferred from the finds. Dates rounded. English Heritage: occupied from the 5th to the mid 7th century, then little activity for over 500 years; Richard of Cornwall acquired the site in 1233. The 1331 decline is from memory.

name: West Stow
summary: A fully excavated early English village, standing here for the thousands of small farming settlements of the 5th to 7th centuries.
uncertainty: Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Sutton Hoo
summary: A mound cemetery above the Deben. The great ship burial of about 625 is most often thought to be that of King Raedwald.
uncertainty: The identity of the dead man is unknown; the date rests on the coins. Start and end of the cemetery are approximate.

name: Rendlesham
summary: Named by Bede as a royal residence; excavation since 2008 has found a large, rich settlement 6 km from Sutton Hoo.
uncertainty: Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Ipswich
summary: One of the four great trading towns (wics) of 7th-9th century England and continuously a town ever since. It was 27th in 1377, 8th in the 1520s and 7th in the 1662 hearth tax.
uncertainty: Foundation in the early 7th century is from excavation, recalled from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Southampton
summary: Hamwic, on the west bank of the Itchen, held perhaps 2,000-3,000 people at its height about 700-850. The walled medieval port grew a little to the south-west.
uncertainty: Hamwic's population is an estimate; the dates of the shift between sites are approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Sandwich
summary: The successor to Richborough as the main port of east Kent, until its haven silted in the 15th and 16th centuries.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Yeavering
summary: A Northumbrian royal centre below the hillfort of Yeavering Bell. In 627 Paulinus spent 36 days here baptising in the River Glen.
uncertainty: Bede says only that it was abandoned under later kings; both dates are approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Bamburgh
summary: The citadel of Bernicia, traditionally taken by Ida in 547, and the base of the English earls who survived north of the Tyne after the Vikings took York.
uncertainty: 547 is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's date and not reliable. 1095 is from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Lindisfarne
summary: Founded in 635 from Iona. Cuthbert died here in 687 and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made about 710-725. Raided on 8 June 793, left for good in 875, and refounded as a cell of Durham by 1122 until its closure in 1537.

name: Jarrow and Wearmouth
summary: Benedict Biscop's 'one monastery in two places', the home of Bede (died 735) and for a time the most learned house in northern Europe.
uncertainty: The marker is at Jarrow; Wearmouth is 10 km to the south-east. English Heritage does not date a Viking attack.

name: Whitby
summary: Founded about 657 and the scene of the synod of 664 that settled the dating of Easter. Abandoned in the 9th century, refounded about 1078 and suppressed in 1539.
uncertainty: The date of abandonment is not known; 867 is nominal.

name: Hexham
summary: Wilfrid's church, built with stone from Roman Corbridge; its 7th-century crypt survives.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Ripon
summary: A Northumbrian monastery whose 7th-century crypt survives under the later minster.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Durham
summary: Cuthbert's relics came to rest here in 995 after the community's long wandering from Lindisfarne by way of Chester-le-Street.
uncertainty: 995 and the foundation stone of 11 August 1093 are confirmed by VCH Durham, which dates the priory's dissolution to 1540; the phase here ends at 1539.

name: Beverley
summary: A minster town which grew into one of the larger towns of medieval England before its cloth trade moved to the West Riding.
uncertainty: Phase dates are approximate. VCH East Riding: John of York buried here in 721; the college and sanctuary are traditionally Athelstan's (930s). Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Tamworth
summary: Mercia had no fixed capital, but its kings issued more charters at Tamworth than anywhere else. A 9th-century watermill has been excavated here.
uncertainty: The start date is nominal; 874 and 913 are Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Repton
summary: A Mercian royal mausoleum. The Great Army wintered here in 873-4, and a D-shaped earthwork and a mass grave of at least 264 people have been excavated.
uncertainty: Monastery foundation date is approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Torksey
summary: The Great Army's camp of 872-3 covered some 55 hectares, larger than most towns of the day.
uncertainty: The size comes from metal-detected finds; dates other than 872-3 are approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Lichfield
summary: The church centre of Mercia and, for sixteen years under Offa, the seat of a third English archbishop.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. 669 is confirmed by VCH Staffordshire; the archbishopric of 787-803 rests on Wikipedia.

name: Worcester
summary: Chosen as the bishop's seat for the kingdom of the Hwicce in 679-680. It was 26th in 1377 and 12th in the 1662 hearth tax.
uncertainty: VCH Worcestershire puts the burh at an unknown date between 872 and 899. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Hereford
summary: The English frontier town against south Wales, burned by a Welsh and Irish force in 1055. Tenth by Russell's Domesday estimate, 21st in 1377.
uncertainty: Early dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Shrewsbury
summary: The chief town of the middle March, 19th in the 1377 poll tax and 14th in 1662.
uncertainty: First recorded in 901 (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Glastonbury
summary: The richest abbey in England at Domesday and again at the Dissolution. Its last abbot was hanged on the Tor in 1539.
uncertainty: A British monastery before about 700 is possible but unproven. Early dates from memory. VCH Somerset accepts King Ine (688-726) as builder of the minster and Dunstan's reform; exact years are approximate. Dissolution date from Wikipedia.

name: Malmesbury
summary: A hilltop abbey and burh; King Aethelstan was buried here in 939.
uncertainty: Foundation date approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Sherborne
summary: Bishop's seat for Wessex west of Selwood from 705 until the Council of London of 1075 moved it to Old Sarum.
uncertainty: 705, the Benedictine refoundation of 998, the removal of the see in 1075 and the surrender of 18 March 1539 are from VCH Dorset.

name: Wells
summary: A cathedral city that never grew large: the church, not trade, was its reason for being.
uncertainty: 909 and the move to Bath in 1088-90 are from VCH Somerset. The 705 minster is tradition; 1180 for the Gothic rebuilding and the joint title of Bath and Wells (1245) are from memory.

name: Athelney
summary: The island fort from which Alfred rallied Wessex in the spring of 878 before Edington.
uncertainty: Abbey date approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Wallingford
summary: Rated at 2,400 hides, the same as Winchester. William crossed the Thames here in 1066. Its Saxon ramparts survive.
uncertainty: The Burghal Hidage is dated to after 914 or, on another view, the 870s-880s; 880 is nominal. VCH Berkshire confirms the Burghal Hidage listing and a castle in being by 1071. The 880 start and the sizes are judgement; ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Wareham
summary: A West Saxon burh of 1,600 hides whose earth ramparts still enclose the town on three sides.
uncertainty: Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Shaftesbury
summary: A burh of 700 hides and the home of the wealthiest house of nuns in medieval England, dissolved in 1539.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Lewes
summary: A burh of 1,300 hides and the chief town of Norman Sussex; about 2,000 people at Domesday.
uncertainty: Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Hastings
summary: A burh of 500 hides which gave its name to the battle fought 10 km inland.
uncertainty: The storm-damage date is approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Oxford
summary: A late Saxon border burh of 1,400 hides which Darby put at about 5,000 people in 1066. Schools gathered here in the 12th century; it was sixteenth in 1377.
uncertainty: 727 is a legendary date. The university's growth from 1167 is the traditional account, from memory. VCH Oxfordshire: first recorded in 911; St Frideswide's house is a tradition placed about the start of the 8th century (727 is her traditional death); by 1066 exceeded only by London, York, Norwich, Lincoln and Winchester. 1167 for the schools is the conventional date, not checked.

name: Cambridge
summary: A river-crossing town where scholars fleeing Oxford settled in 1209; they had a chancellor by 1226. It was 22nd in 1377.
uncertainty: Roman and Danish dates approximate. 875, the castle of 1068 and the clerks first mentioned in 1209 are in VCH Cambridgeshire.

name: Norwich
summary: Not a Roman town: it grew from the 10th century and Darby gives it about 6,500 people in 1066. Sixth in 1377, it was second only to London in the 1520s and in 1662.
uncertainty: The move of the bishopric from Thetford in 1094 is from memory. Sizes are relative ranks. VCH Norfolk: see moved from Thetford by Herbert de Losinga, cathedral foundation stone laid 1096. Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia; the pre-1066 phases are judgement.

name: Thetford
summary: Sixth largest town in Domesday England and briefly a cathedral city, then eclipsed by Norwich.
uncertainty: The priory dates (founded 1103-4, surrendered February 1540) are from English Heritage and VCH Norfolk; VCH also records the bishop's move from Thetford to Norwich under Herbert de Losinga. The 1072 start of the see and the town's ranking still rest on Wikipedia.

name: Bury St Edmunds
summary: One of the richest abbeys in England, built over the body of the East Anglian king killed by the Danes in 869. Fifteenth in 1377.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. 903 (or a little later), 1020 and the surrender of 4 November 1539 are from VCH Suffolk. Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Ely
summary: A fen-island monastery that became one of the great cathedrals; 23rd in the 1377 poll tax.
uncertainty: 673, 870, 970, 1109 and the surrender of 18 November 1539 are confirmed by VCH Cambridgeshire. The 1377 rank follows a table reported on Wikipedia.

name: Peterborough
summary: A fen-edge abbey whose monks kept the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle going until 1154.
uncertainty: 655-6, 870, the refoundation of about 966 (finished 972) and the surrender of 1539 are from VCH Northamptonshire. 1541 for the new see is from memory.

name: Derby
summary: A Danish army base taken by Aethelflaed in 917.
uncertainty: The capture date is from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Nottingham
summary: One of the Five Boroughs; 29th in the 1377 poll tax.
uncertainty: 868 and 1068 from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Stamford
summary: A Danelaw borough which Darby put at about 3,000 people in 1086.
uncertainty: Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Northampton
summary: A favoured meeting place of 12th-century kings and councils; 28th in 1377.
uncertainty: Phase dates approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Warwick
summary: Listed at 2,400 hides in the later Burghal Hidage manuscripts.
uncertainty: 914 and 1068 from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Old Sarum
summary: A hillfort of about 400 BCE reused for a mint in 1003, a Norman castle and a cathedral (see moved here 1075). The clergy left for the new city of Salisbury in the 1220s.
uncertainty: The date of final desertion is approximate.

name: Salisbury
summary: Founded in 1220 to replace Old Sarum. It was eighth in the 1377 poll tax and seventh by wealth in the 1520s.
uncertainty: Phase boundaries are approximate. VCH Wiltshire: churchyard consecrated 1219, cathedral consecrated 1258.

name: Bristol
summary: First heard of about 1000. Third in the 1377 poll tax and in the 1520s, and the starting point of English Atlantic voyages from the 1480s.
uncertainty: Start date approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Coventry
summary: The great boom town of the 14th-century Midlands; it then lost perhaps half its people between about 1440 and 1520 and was 19th in 1662.
uncertainty: VCH Warwickshire: priory founded about 1043, 4,817 poll-tax payers in 1377 (behind only London, Bristol and York on one reckoning), 6,601 people counted in 1520 and 565 houses empty in 1523. The 1601 step down is a judgement; ranks in the 1520s and 1662 follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Plymouth
summary: The base of Drake and Hawkins and the port the fleet sailed from against the Armada in 1588.
uncertainty: Russell's 1377 poll tax figures put Plymouth fourth in England, which is hard to reconcile with other evidence and may reflect soldiers and seamen; the size 4 phase follows that figure with reserve. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: King's Lynn
summary: The outlet for the whole Great Ouse basin. Ninth in 1377 and ninth by wealth in the 1520s.
uncertainty: Founded about 1100 by Bishop Losinga (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Boston
summary: At its 13th-century peak Boston exported more wool than any other English port. Eleventh in 1377.
uncertainty: The 13th-century ranking is from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Great Yarmouth
summary: A town built on a sandspit that formed across the Roman-period estuary. Twentieth in 1377, eighth in 1662.
uncertainty: Phase dates approximate. English Heritage confirms a trading quay from at least the 12th century and a 13th-century boom; the phase years are judgement. Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Dunwich
summary: One of the largest ports of the east coast in the 12th and 13th centuries. Storms in 1286, 1287, 1328, 1347 and 1362 destroyed most of it and shifted its river mouth.
uncertainty: The identification with Dommoc is disputed (Walton Castle is the alternative). The medieval town lies under the sea, so the marker is at the surviving village. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Ravenser Odd
summary: A 13th-century boom port off Spurn Head which sent members to the parliament of 1295 and was drowned in the winter storms of 1356-62.
uncertainty: The site has not been found; the position is approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Winchelsea
summary: Edward I's replacement for Old Winchelsea, which the sea destroyed in 1287. Much of its street grid was never filled.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Kingston upon Hull
summary: Bought by Edward I in 1293 as a northern supply port. It was 25th in 1377 and 18th in 1662.
uncertainty: Early dates from memory. VCH East Riding confirms Edward I's acquisition of Wyke from Meaux Abbey in 1293; the 1193 first mention is not checked.

name: Newcastle upon Tyne
summary: Named from Robert Curthose's castle of 1080. It was 13th in 1377 and 4th in the 1520s, by then sending coal by sea to London.
uncertainty: The Roman fort is later than the bridge; 122 stands for both. Hadrian's Wall was begun in 122 (English Heritage). Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Berwick-upon-Tweed
summary: A Scottish town for most of the Middle Ages, finally taken by England in 1482. It is listed under England only for that last phase.
uncertainty: 1296, 1318, 1482 and the ramparts (begun 1558, stopped 1569) are English Heritage's dates. The 1120 start as a royal burgh is from memory.

name: Scarborough
summary: One of a chain of late 4th-century coastal watchtowers, later a major royal castle.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. English Heritage: signal station of the late 4th century; castle begun probably in the 1130s by William le Gros and rebuilt by Henry II from 1159. A chapel stood on the headland by about 1000, so 'deserted' is too strong for the 11th century.

name: Portsmouth
summary: A minor port until Henry VII built a dry dock here in 1495; the Mary Rose sank offshore in 1545.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Dartmouth
summary: A Devon port for the Bordeaux wine trade, privateering and later the Newfoundland fishery.
uncertainty: Start date is the first recorded fleet assembly, from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Bodmin
summary: The chief church of Cornwall after its bishops moved east, and a rallying point of the risings of 1497 and 1549.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Reading
summary: A small town transformed by Henry I's abbey of 1121, dissolved in 1539 when its abbot was hanged.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Lavenham
summary: A Suffolk village that briefly paid more tax than York, on the strength of its blue broadcloth.
uncertainty: Phase dates approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Walsingham
summary: The second pilgrim shrine of medieval England after Canterbury.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Battle Abbey
summary: Founded by William about 1071 on the site of his victory, consecrated in 1094 and surrendered in May 1538.

name: Fountains Abbey
summary: The richest Cistercian house in England, dissolved in 1539.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Rievaulx Abbey
summary: Founded in March 1132. Under Aelred it held 140 monks and about 500 lay brothers. It was shut down on 3 December 1538.
uncertainty: The date of the fall in numbers is nominal.

name: Furness Abbey
summary: In 1537 the first of the larger houses to be dissolved by voluntary surrender.
uncertainty: Foundation date from memory. 1127 (after a first settlement at Tulketh in 1124), the Cistercian takeover of 1147 and the surrender of 9 April 1537 are English Heritage's dates.

name: Windsor Castle
summary: One of the ring of castles William built around London, and a main royal residence from the 12th century.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Kenilworth Castle
summary: Begun about 1120. It withstood a six-month siege in 1266, was rebuilt as a palace by John of Gaunt from 1371, and entertained Elizabeth I in 1575.
uncertainty: The 1210 and 1563 phase dates are from memory.

name: Corfe Castle
summary: One of the earliest stone castles in England and a favourite stronghold of King John.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Ludlow
summary: A Lacy and Mortimer castle which became the administrative capital of Wales and the border counties from 1472.
uncertainty: Castle begun about 1086-94 (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Pontefract Castle
summary: The strongest castle in Yorkshire.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Richmond Castle
summary: Built after the Harrying of the North to hold the lands of the former English earl; among the oldest stone castles in England.
uncertainty: Date from memory. English Heritage: land granted to Alan about 1071 and the castle begun soon afterwards.

name: Alnwick Castle
summary: The stronghold of the Percy earls of Northumberland, the dominant family of the far north.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Framlingham Castle
summary: Where Mary Tudor gathered her supporters and was proclaimed queen in 1553.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. English Heritage calls it a late 12th-century castle built by Roger Bigod; an earlier castle from about 1100 is not confirmed by the page fetched.

name: Clarendon Palace
summary: A favourite residence of Henry II and Henry III; the Constitutions of Clarendon were issued here in 1164.
uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Hampton Court
summary: The best surviving Tudor royal palace; the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 commissioned the King James Bible.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Nonsuch Palace
summary: Begun in 1538 to rival the French king's châteaux; pulled down in the 1680s.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Liverpool
summary: Still a town of a few hundred people in 1625. Included to show how small the later great port was.
uncertainty: Charter date from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Leeds
summary: A village with a borough attached until woollen cloth-making made it a town in the 16th century; incorporated in 1626.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Birmingham
summary: Granted a market in 1166; by the 1530s Leland heard its smiths from the road.
uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Kendal
summary: The main cloth town of the north-west.
uncertainty: Dates nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Battle of Dyrham
summary: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says the West Saxons killed three British kings here and took Gloucester, Cirencester and Bath.
uncertainty: Written down three centuries later; many historians doubt the details. Location follows the place-name. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Battle of Ellendun
summary: Egbert of Wessex defeated Beornwulf of Mercia; Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex passed to Wessex and Mercian dominance ended.
uncertainty: Usually placed at Wroughton near Swindon; the exact field is unknown. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Battle of Edington
summary: In May 878 Alfred defeated Guthrum's army, which then accepted baptism and withdrew to East Anglia.
uncertainty: Probably Edington in Wiltshire; the site has been argued over for centuries. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Battle of Brunanburh
summary: Aethelstan defeated the allied kings of Dublin, Scotland and Strathclyde, securing the new kingdom of the English.
uncertainty: The location is unknown: over forty sites have been proposed. The marker is at Bromborough on the Wirral, the most widely supported candidate. Date (late 937) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as unlocated.

name: Battle of Maldon
summary: Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex was killed fighting a Viking fleet on 10 or 11 August 991; payments of tribute followed.
uncertainty: The causeway to Northey Island fits the Old English poem best but is not proven. Date (10 (possibly 11) August 991) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably on the mainland opposite Northey Island, though other sites have been suggested. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Maldon 991' (list entry 1000019).

name: Battle of Brentford
summary: Edmund Ironside crossed the Thames at Brentford two days after relieving London and drove Cnut's army off, at heavy cost to his own men.
uncertainty: Known mainly from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; the exact ground and the month are uncertain. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Battle of Assandun
summary: On 18 October 1016 Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside; Edmund died weeks later and Cnut took the whole kingdom.
uncertainty: Either Ashingdon (shown) or Ashdon, both in Essex; the question is open. Date (18 October 1016) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as unlocated.

name: Battle of Fulford
summary: On 20 September 1066 Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar outside York.
uncertainty: The exact field is disputed. Date (20 September 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located around Germany Beck and Fulford Ings.

name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
summary: On 25 September 1066 Harold Godwinson surprised and killed Harald Hardrada and Tostig.
uncertainty: Date (25 September 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as different interpretations of where the battle was fought have been suggested. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Stamford Bridge 1066' (list entry 1000035).

name: Battle of Hastings
summary: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold. Battle Abbey was founded on the site about 1071.
uncertainty: Date (14 October 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably accurately located in the fields south of Battle Abbey. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Hastings 1066' (list entry 1000013).

name: Battle of the Standard
summary: On 22 August 1138 a northern English army raised by Archbishop Thurstan defeated David I of Scotland near Northallerton.
uncertainty: Date (22 August 1138) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably accurately located north of Northallerton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Northallerton 1138' (list entry 1000027).

name: Battle of Lewes
